title: The return of Eddy Current Suppression Ring on Breaking and Entering
summary: Almost ten years after their last release, Melbourne’s much-loved Eddy Current Suppression Ring have put out a new album, All in Good Time. Breaking and Entering’s Lauren and Simon chat with Brendan and Mikey of the band about the record. They share the impetus for recording the new material, how their respective careers in visual arts and audio mixing informed the album making process, plus some of their favorite tracks from 2019.
transcript:
Brendan Huntley and Mikey Young of Eddy Current Suppression Ring joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios to discuss All in Good Time, returning to writing together and their music selections for 2019. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, 12 December 2019, the day before the album’s release. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Do I call you Brendan Suppression?

Brendan: Let's go with Brendan Suppression.

Lauren: Brendan, congratulations on the newest arrival to your family, Oberon. How have you been adjusting to parenthood?

Brendan: I'm still figuring that out, but it's rad. It's wild.

Lauren: You shared a name poem your brother wrote. Can you tell us about the significance of that?

Brendan: Yeah, I guess I can. It's Wilsons Promontory. There's a mountain, Mount Oberon, and Wilsons Prom is just very special to myself and my partner. It just felt like a great name for the little human being that came into our world. My brother, he's a bit of a lyrics man himself, a poet. So he put that out there to me, and I was like, 'It's nice.' That's what that's about.

Lauren: Mikey, you've just got back from a Total Control tour overseas?

Mikey: Yeah. What day is it? Three days ago, I think. Six shows in Japan and one in Vietnam.

Lauren: After almost ten years, Eddy Current Suppression Ring have a new album. The band famously started writing together at a Christmas party. When did you realise an album was starting to take shape?

Brendan: I guess it all started post Golden Plains. What's that, three years ago?

Mikey: Well, even pre, because we were kind of jamming.

Brendan: Oh yeah, we were jamming.

Mikey: When we got asked to do that, we were all forced to jam. We've always hung out with each other individually, but I think we realised it'd been so long since we actually just all hung out together. It was like, 'The only way you can force yourself to do that is just organise band practice all the time.' After Golden Plains, Danny got really busy with his new tattoo shop. So me, Brad and Brendan just kept jamming at each other's houses with a drum machine. We were making really quiet songs, and we recorded them. We were like, 'Maybe this is a different thing. We'll just call this something else.' We sat with them for a bit, and we were just like, 'These songs would be kind of better with Danny on them, I reckon.' I think that was the impetus. After that amount of time, I think Danny had kind of quietened down a little.

Mikey: We all had some spare time, and we just started booking a jam in Frankston every fortnight or so. We were going over those older songs and then accidentally writing new songs until we had like twelve songs. It was like, 'We might as well try and record them.'

Brendan: Twelve or fourteen. Maybe fourteen even.

Mikey: Even then, which was probably June, I don't think we thought we were going to make a record. It was just like, 'We'll see if they're any good.' Because sometimes you think things are good, and then you listen back and it's not as good as you thought. I went away mid-year, came back and mixed it. It wasn't until mid-September that they were all ready. I was like, 'I think there's at least maybe eleven of these that are okay.' Then we just put it together. I was like, 'I think it kind of works.' I think the day after it was finished, I emailed John at Castle Face and just said, 'Do you want to put this out?' He was like, 'Sure. What about May next year?' I was like, 'What about December?' He said, 'No one puts out a record in December, but fuck it. Let's do it anyway.'

Simon: That euphoric return at Golden Plains sparked and rekindled that?

Brendan: I think the spark was already kind of weirdly growing. So when that was offered, it was like, 'Well, this is a nice time.' There were already a couple of little things there that were reminding us just of how good it is to be together. The playing part at Golden Plains was pretty phenomenal, so it cemented that thought.

Simon: All in Good Time arrives ten years after Rush to Relax. Has the lead-up to putting out this new record been a reflective time for you, Mikey?

Mikey: Not really. I think it feels pretty separate. It was kind of weird because it happened in a bubble that didn't involve crowds or road-testing songs to people. I think there was a little bit of habit, when I was mixing it, to reflect on the old albums and make sure we weren't ruining whatever kind of legacy we might have had by adding a shitty album onto it. I think I managed to separate it and just not worry about it.

Lauren: What about sonically? Were you listening back to make sure it fitted in?

Mikey: Kind of, but only at the end. I was like, 'Have I done something better or worse here?' I'd listen to it, and I was like, 'It kind of sounds exactly the same.' Once it came to the thought that maybe we'd put this out there, it was a weird pressure to think people were going to judge this against those things, and people were going to reflect in their own ways. But it really did feel like a totally different thing.

Simon: Brendan, was there a liberation in that separation from what Eddy Current were doing at the start of the decade and the live community there at the time?

Brendan: Any time I'm writing lyrics, I'm not thinking about how they're going to be perceived live or what people will think of them. It's really just what these guys will feel with them, and that's always been pretty accepted. I took a little bit of a breather from lyric-writing for a while there. When the Golden Plains gig came up, it was around the same time I was feeling more fluid with lyrics. That, for me, is basically what fuels me if I've got something to bring to the table. The more you jam, the more excited you are. You're going home and bringing more and more. That fuels the fire kind of thing.

Brendan: Does that answer it? Did I answer your question?

Simon: It definitely does. Lauren and I have been following your activity in the visual-art world and the work you've been posting on Instagram. One post featured a photo of an old gig, a Super8 fundraiser.

Brendan: I was reminiscing.

Simon: With this being the end of the decade, and that being before the release of Rush to Relax, is there a sense of how far Eddy Current has come and its place in the musical community of Melbourne?

Brendan: I try not to think too much about any of that, apart from, 'That was a great memory.' When someone sends a photo like that, you're like, 'Oh man, that felt like yesterday.' The rest of it's just kind of rad that that's been part of my life. I am that person, but I don't know. Just try and take a day at a time. I like nostalgia, but not getting too stuck in it. Do you know what I mean?

Simon: Your visual art spans painting, drawing and sculpture. Your partner Ellen wrote about the physical process of creation for you: 'To interrupt Brendan while he's making art is akin to shaking someone out of a deep and pleasant dream.' How does that process of creation in visual art relate to lyric-writing?

Brendan: It's the same brain, but I don't think too much about that. Whenever I'm in the zone with whatever it is, I try and stay on it. You might be working on a painting or something and then leave it for a few days and come back to it. I find with lyrics, most of the time, if I can get the majority done in that burst, it's going to be a better song, lyrically. I don't know why. I'm in the heat of it. Whereas with sculpture or painting, you can chip away at it a little more. But then again, thinking about it, I'll bring some lyrics to the jam, and then Mikey might have something, and I'll have to change it around, or new ideas will start flowing out there. Or it might be one verse that I've come in with, but then the rest kind of comes there. I just kind of get in the moment.

Lauren: You were both mentioning before we came on air how some songs on this album were a process of addition and subtraction, and others seemed to come together extremely quickly. Can you talk about some of those studio sessions where things seemed to cohere?

Mikey: I think the actual songwriting is quite quick. Maybe we'll chop and change lengths and stuff, but I think the best songs we write, or at least the ones we keep, always happen pretty instantaneously. I think we're not a very good band at working hard on things. It's either just not very good—

Brendan: Or maybe all the hard work comes in the preparation.

Mikey: Yeah, maybe. We're aware of what we like and what we're good at, maybe. I think for me it's more the process after that. We should be a really simple band to mix because there's only four things. I try to keep it simple because I don't really like to add too many things when I'm mixing it. But sometimes what I thought the song sounded like, or I thought some part really kicked in and sounded amazing, you listen back and say, 'I'm not really feeling what I thought we did in this song.' So just getting the balance of things to sound like what our intentions were, maybe. I think that's where it gets a little difficult. Some songs take one hour to mix, and I'm just like, 'Well, that was easy.' They're the songs I love the most because I didn't hassle myself about it. But the songs that don't sound like what I thought they were like are the hardest for me to love because maybe I spent too long analysing their faults or something. It's probably not the problems the rest of the band go through because they're like, 'I like this song.' It's more just stupid things I do in my own time.

Mikey: None of it really matters. People just go, 'Yeah, good song.'

Simon: Mikey, we've spoken about compilations you've made, Follow the Sun and this year's Sad About the Times. Both sought to capture a particular time in history. You've been living through another era of music as a maker, and mixing and mastering. How would you tell the story of this current era? What would the compilation sound like if you were to make a document of this time?

Mikey: I don't know. I've been asked to do that before, to make more current-day comps, and I've backed out because I don't feel like I'm the right man to do it. Maybe because modern music has become my day job, I don't feel that distance from it that I can sit back as a listener and a lover of music. It's probably made me gravitate to older music because it seems otherworldly, and it has nothing to do with me and my surroundings. Especially when I'm working on music and mixing and mastering, I don't have that separation or that immediate love for things because I'm analysing it too much. That's why I just don't think I could. I think you guys would make a much better comp of current music than I would.

Lauren: Do you feel like an anthropologist when you're mixing, mastering, producing and making music? Do you hear certain movements or sounds that seem to tell a story of a time or place that you find intriguing?

Mikey: I definitely hear things come in and out of fashion. Maybe fashion is the wrong word. I do hear people around the world gravitating towards a sound or a feeling. When I started, I was probably just getting every local garage band. Now I get jazz records to work on, or bands from the Netherlands, or hardcore bands or electronic stuff. I guess the patterns don't seem that apparent to me because my work's just become crazily diverse.

Lauren: We've been looking back at some of our favourite songs from 2019 and asked you to bring a few of your selections. Mikey, we've got 'Dad Cry' by TAWINGS lined up. Can you talk us through this one?

Mikey: I don't know much about this at all, and it's not something I've thought too long and hard about. I just got back from tour in Japan, and at one of our shows a DJ was playing this. I'm not really much of a DJ pest usually, but I was just like, 'What the hell is this?' It just sounds like the first B-52's album or something. I wrote it down. I've only been back home a couple of days, so I'm kind of all hyped on things I heard just recently, and this seemed like a pretty good opportunity to play it.

Lauren: Brendan, we just heard your selection there. Can you talk us through it?

Brendan: I wouldn't even say it's my favourite, but it was just sent to me from Rick from Boomgates the other day on my phone. I listened to it. I was like, 'This is great. It's new, so it suits what you guys are doing.' I thought it was good. I don't know anything about them, apart from the fact that they're from Serbia, Belgrade.

Simon: Krava 22.

Brendan: Yeah, I think so.

Lauren: Do you have an informal music-sharing network going on on text?

Brendan: Yeah, pretty informal. It's usually one-way. The way I listen to music, I don't know when it's from most of the time. It could be a bunch of rap for a bit, and then whatever. So this was just on the top of my mind, you know what I mean?

Simon: Mikey, we heard one of yours at the top. Is it TAWINGS?

Mikey: Yeah, TAWINGS. I think that's how you say it.

Simon: I think that came out on a seven-inch a couple of years ago, as far as I can tell. I think their first album just came out or is just about to come out.

Mikey: I don't know much about them either.

Simon: From Tokyo?

Mikey: Yeah.

Lauren: Will you be doing some shows next year? What is going to happen?

Mikey: I think we're all going to have a little catch-up dinner next week. I don't know. If people like the record and we feel like it, it would be nice to play them live. But I can't imagine we'll ever get too insanely active again. It would be nice to do something.

Brendan: There's no plans right now.

Mikey: Yeah, we've got to have a chat.

Lauren: We're going to end with one of your selections, Mikey. Can you talk us through Klan Aileen?

Mikey: This is just another, 'I just heard this while I was away, and it sounds good, and it's on the top of my head.' We were playing our first show in Tokyo. This really nice guy came up with a really well-wrapped parcel of two jumpers and five CDs with their personal stamp on it. He said, 'I'm a big fan. I want you to listen to my band.' I was super touched. I only got a chance to listen to it when I got home on Monday. I think I listened to it Tuesday. It's all really good, but there was this one really nice long instrumental that was really beautiful. That record came out this year, and I think someone told me they've got a next record coming out on Captured Tracks or something like that. Anyway, all I can tell you is he's a nice guy.
